promptText: What mechanism does React Router use to change the URL and swap the rendered UI without a full page reload?
options: It calls history.pushState to update the URL and matches the new path against the route config to render the matching component
It sends an XHR request to the server for a new HTML document and replaces the DOM with a diff of the response
It reloads the page but caches the previous DOM tree so the transition appears instant
It relies on the browser's native anchor-tag navigation with the target attribute set to "_self"
explanation: React Router intercepts navigation, calls history.pushState to update the address bar without a network request, and matches the new URL against the route config to render the corresponding component tree, listening to popstate for Back/Forward.

promptText: Why is `<div onClick={() => navigate('/x')}>` considered an anti-pattern compared to `<Link to="/x">`?
options: It loses semantic anchor behavior — no href for middle-click/open-in-new-tab, no right-click 'copy link,' and broken keyboard and screen-reader accessibility
onClick handlers cannot call useNavigate from inside a React component
navigate() always triggers a full page reload, while Link never does
Link requires an ApolloProvider higher in the tree while a plain onClick handler does not
explanation: Link renders a real anchor element, so it gets href-based behaviors (middle-click to open in a new tab, right-click to copy the link, keyboard focus, screen reader semantics) for free — a div with a click handler reinvents navigation without any of that.

promptText: Why does a route defined as /users/:id require you to manually coerce useParams().id before using it as a number?
options: Route params are always returned as strings (or undefined), regardless of what the URL segment looks like numerically
useParams only returns numbers, so string ids must be manually re-stringified before use
useParams re-parses the entire URL synchronously on every keystroke, returning a fresh string each time
TypeScript automatically converts params to numbers, but only when strict mode is enabled
explanation: Every value useParams() returns is a string (or undefined) since it comes directly from a URL segment; validating and converting it (e.g. Number(id)) is the caller's responsibility.

promptText: What happens if a parent route's element forgets to render an `<Outlet />`?
options: The child route still matches internally, but nothing for it actually renders on screen
React Router throws a build-time error and refuses to compile the app
The child route automatically renders itself outside the parent's DOM tree
The parent route's own content stops rendering entirely
explanation: Outlet is the placeholder where a matched child route's element is substituted; without it, the child route still matches (the URL is valid) but there's nowhere for its content to be inserted, so nothing appears.

promptText: Why should a redirect from an unauthenticated /dashboard visit to /login use replace instead of the default push navigation?
options: With push, pressing Back from the login page would return to /dashboard, which the guard immediately redirects away from again, creating a broken back-button loop
Replace navigations are the only ones that support passing a state object
Push navigations cannot be triggered from inside a Navigate component
Replace is required for React Router to apply the errorElement correctly
explanation: Push adds a new history entry, so Back would return to the protected page that just redirected the user away, causing a loop; replace swaps the current entry so Back skips over the failed attempt entirely.

promptText: In nested routes that each fetch their own data, why do useEffect-based fetches create a worse waterfall than data-router loaders?
options: Each nested component's effect only fires after it mounts, which requires its parent to render first, so nested fetches happen serially; loaders for the whole matched branch run concurrently at navigation time
useEffect fetches are synchronous and block the main thread, while loaders always run in a Web Worker
Loaders cannot fetch data for more than one route at a time, making them slower for nested routes
useEffect fetches are automatically cached by React, while loaders never cache anything
explanation: A useEffect fetch waits for its own component to mount, which itself waits on the parent rendering first — a serial chain across nested routes. The data router instead matches the whole route branch up front and calls every matched loader concurrently.

promptText: A team believes wrapping /admin routes in a client-side RequireAuth guard is sufficient to secure admin data. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Client-side guards only control what renders in the browser; a user can call the underlying API endpoints directly, so the server must independently authorize every request regardless of what the client guard decided
RequireAuth components cannot be nested more than one level deep in React Router's route tree
Guards only work with the classic <Routes> API and are silently ignored by createBrowserRouter
Client guards make an extra network request that is slower than simply not protecting the route at all
explanation: A route guard is a UX layer that decides what to render — it's trivially bypassed by calling the API directly with dev tools, so the actual security boundary must be enforced server-side on every request, independent of what the client-side router decided.

promptText: By default, what happens to a page's loaders after any action completes successfully in the data router, and why might that be wasteful?
options: React Router automatically re-runs every currently rendered route's loaders (revalidation), which can needlessly refetch data for routes whose content the mutation didn't actually affect
Only the loader belonging to the exact route that defined the action re-runs; every sibling loader is left stale
All loaders are cleared from cache and never refetch again until the user manually calls revalidate()
Actions trigger a full browser reload to guarantee data consistency
explanation: Automatic revalidation re-runs every currently rendered route's loader after a successful action by default, which keeps the UI in sync but can be wasteful for loaders whose data the mutation never actually touched — shouldRevalidate lets you opt specific routes out.

promptText: Why can't a shared useNavigation() hook provide independent per-item pending state for 50 separate 'like' buttons in a list?
options: useNavigation reflects one global, router-wide navigation state, so all 50 buttons would see the same pending flag instead of each tracking its own in-flight request — useFetcher gives each button its own independent state
useNavigation can only be called once per application, so it cannot be used inside list items at all
useNavigation only reports state for GET requests, never for form submissions or mutations
useFetcher and useNavigation are functionally identical, so this isn't actually a real limitation
explanation: useNavigation is global and reflects the router's overall navigation state, so it can't distinguish which of 50 buttons is in flight; useFetcher creates an independent instance with its own state, data, and Form scoped to just that one component.

promptText: Since React Router v6, why can renaming a route's URL segment sometimes NOT break `<Link to="..">` calls inside it, unlike naive string-based relative paths?
options: Relative link resolution in v6 is route-tree-relative by default, resolving against the matched route structure rather than doing raw string math on the current URL's segments
v6 removed relative link support entirely, so all links must use absolute paths
to=".." in v6 always navigates to the application root regardless of nesting depth
v6 stores every link's destination in a lookup table generated at build time
explanation: v6's default relative resolution is based on the route tree structure, not the literal URL string, so renaming a path segment doesn't break relative links defined against that route — you can opt into the older URL-segment-based behavior with relative="path" when needed.

promptText: Why might a list page's default ScrollRestoration behavior jump back to the top every time a user changes a filter or sort option, and how do you fix it?
options: Scroll position is keyed by a value that changes on every navigation, including query-param-only changes; passing a custom getKey that returns just the pathname groups all query-string variants together so scroll position persists across filter changes
ScrollRestoration can only preserve scroll position on the very first page load and never afterward
The only fix is disabling ScrollRestoration entirely, since it exposes no configuration options
Filter changes always force a full browser page reload, which is why scroll resets regardless of ScrollRestoration
explanation: By default ScrollRestoration keys saved positions by location.key, which changes on every navigation including query-only changes; a custom getKey keyed on pathname alone groups query-string variants of the same page so scroll position survives filter/sort changes.

promptText: Why does modeling auth status as "loading" | "authenticated" | "unauthenticated" (three states) avoid a bug that a plain boolean isAuthenticated flag does not?
options: A two-state model collapses 'not yet known' into 'false,' causing a guard to redirect to login prematurely and then bounce back once the async session check actually resolves as authenticated
React hooks require at least three possible state values to avoid infinite render loops
A boolean flag cannot be read inside a route loader, only inside React components
Three-state models are mandated by TypeScript's strict null checks for any auth-related state
explanation: On a hard refresh, auth status often starts unknown before an async session check resolves; a two-state boolean treats 'not yet known' as 'false' and redirects to login, then has to redirect back once the check confirms the user is logged in — a jarring flash the third 'loading' state avoids.

promptText: A login page reads a ?next= query param and calls navigate(next) after a successful login without validating it. What vulnerability does this introduce, and what is the fix?
options: An attacker can craft a login link with ?next=https://evil.example.com, turning the trusted login flow into an open redirect to a phishing site; the fix is validating that next is a same-origin relative path before navigating to it
It causes an infinite redirect loop between the login page and itself, eventually crashing the browser tab
It exposes the user's session token directly in the URL, which is fixed by switching the login form from GET to POST
It has no real security impact since React Router automatically escapes every navigate() target
explanation: An unvalidated next param is a classic open-redirect vector — an attacker crafts a link through your trusted login domain that ultimately bounces the user to an external phishing site; the fix is checking the value is a same-origin relative path (e.g. starts with a single "/") before trusting it.

promptText: A team wraps every routed page in both a route-level errorElement and a separate traditional React class-component error boundary around each page, believing both are necessary for full coverage. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: errorElement already catches both loader/action errors and render errors thrown within its route, making the traditional boundary redundant inside the route tree — a classic boundary is only still useful for errors outside the routed tree, such as the app shell wrapping RouterProvider itself
errorElement can only catch render errors, never loader or action errors, so the traditional boundary is the only thing actually catching data-fetching failures
Traditional React error boundaries automatically disable any errorElement present in the same app, so only one of the two will ever fire
Neither mechanism can coexist in the same application; React Router throws a configuration error if both are used together
explanation: React Router wraps each routed element in its own internal error boundary, so errorElement is a superset for anything inside its route — it catches loader/action errors (which a plain componentDidCatch boundary cannot see at all) and render errors from that route's component tree; a classic boundary only earns its place outside the routed tree entirely.

promptText: After deploying a new build, a user with an old tab open navigates to a lazy-loaded route and hits a chunk-load failure because the old chunk hash no longer exists on the server. What is the correct, safe fix?
options: Detect the chunk-load error in the route's error boundary and force window.location.reload() to fetch the fresh app, guarded by a one-shot flag (e.g. in sessionStorage) so a genuinely broken app doesn't trap the user in an infinite reload loop
Increase the chunk cache duration on the CDN indefinitely so old chunks are never evicted
Always retry the same dynamic import() call up to 10 times, since retries alone resolve chunk-hash mismatches
Disable route-based code splitting entirely so this class of failure becomes structurally impossible
explanation: A stale chunk hash after a deploy can't be fixed by retrying the same broken URL; the real fix is detecting the chunk-load failure and reloading the page to fetch the current index.html and manifest — but that reload must be guarded with a one-shot flag, or a genuinely broken app traps the user in an endless reload cycle.
